title: What's wrong? — body, weather and bị
goal: Describe aches and the weather, and master the pair *bị* and *được* — two words that mark whether something happens to you for the worse or for the better.
bekal: describing complaints with *bị* + condition and *đau* + body part
telling *bị* (something bad happens to you) from *được* (something good comes your way)
talking about the weather with *trời* as the subject

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ở hiệu thuốc
dialogs.intro: A small pharmacy at the end of an alley. Budi has been feeling unwell for two days, and in Vietnam the pharmacy is where people go first, before a doctor.

lines.speaker: Dược sĩ:
lines.text: Chào anh, anh cần gì ạ?
lines.baca: Chào ang, ang kần gì ạ?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Em bị đau đầu và hơi sốt ạ.
lines.id: I have a headache and a bit of a fever.
lines.literal: younger-sibling suffer ache head and slightly fever (polite).

lines.text: Hai ngày rồi ạ. Đêm qua em bị mất ngủ.

lines.text: Có, hơi ho ạ. Chắc tại trời lạnh.

notes: **Bị marks that something unpleasant happens to you**, and it stands before the condition: *bị đau đầu* (have a headache), *bị ốm* (be sick), *bị mất ví* (lose your wallet), *bị phạt* (get fined). English does something similar with "get" — *get fined*, *get caught in the rain* — so you already know the idea.

**Được is its twin for pleasant things**: *được nghỉ* (get time off), *được khen* (be praised), *được tăng lương* (get a raise). Swapping them sounds funny: *bị tăng lương* means roughly "unfortunately, I got a raise".

**Đau means "hurt, ache", and the body part follows right after it**: *đau đầu* (headache), *đau bụng* (stomachache), *đau răng* (toothache). Just like English "head-ache", only in reverse order. The word *ốm* means "sick" in the general sense of unwell.

**Trời means "sky", and it's the subject of every weather sentence**: *trời mưa* (it's raining), *trời nắng* (it's sunny and hot), *trời lạnh* (it's cold). Literally "the sky rains" — the same job English gives to "it". Vietnamese has no separate verb "to rain" without it.

**Thế nào? means "how?"** and it sits at the end of the sentence like other question words: *Em uống thế nào?* (how do I take it?), *Phở thế nào?* (how's the phở?). Its southern cousin is *sao?* — *Sao rồi?* ("how's it going?").

**Sau khi means "after" and trước khi means "before"**, and both are followed by a verb: *sau khi ăn* (after eating), *trước khi ngủ* (before sleeping). *Khi* alone means "when, the time", so it's literally "after the time of eating".

grammars.title: Bị and được — two doors for things that happen to you
body: Vietnamese has no passive like English "be + -ed". Instead there are two words that mark the **feel** of the event: bad or good. The choice is required, and picking the wrong one is instantly noticeable.
after: ⚠️ **What decides it isn't grammar but your own view of the event.** The same sentence can take either: *được đi Hà Nội* (get the chance to go to Hà Nội — happy) versus *bị đi Hà Nội* (be made to go to Hà Nội — reluctant). Vietnamese makes you state your feelings, and that's what makes these words feel so alive.

*Bị* is also used to ask how long a complaint has lasted: *Bị mấy ngày rồi?* ("for how many days?"). Notice the verb isn't repeated — *bị* alone is enough, since the complaint has already been mentioned.

grammars.title: Parts of the body
body: To complain, two words are enough: *đau* + the body part. There are no other forms to learn.
after: ⚠️ *Người* means "person" **and** "body": *Người tôi mệt quá.* = "my body is so tired". A word you've known since unit 1 turns out to have a second job — a pattern typical of a language where almost every word is one syllable.
*Tay* means both hand **and** arm; *chân* means both foot **and** leg. Vietnamese doesn't split them the way English does (*hand/arm*, *foot/leg*) — context tells you which one is meant.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Northern Vietnam has four seasons, the south only two.** Hà Nội gets genuinely cold in *mùa đông* — down to ten degrees Celsius, and homes there rarely have heating, so bring a jacket. Sài Gòn knows only *mùa mưa* and *mùa khô*, like the rest of tropical Southeast Asia. If you're learning the language for travel, this is the difference you'll feel most.
*Trở* means "turn, become": *trời trở lạnh* (it's turned cold), *trời trở nóng*. And to ask, just say *Hôm nay trời thế nào?* — "what's the weather like today?"

blocks.title: The pharmacy is the first stop
items: In Vietnam, the *hiệu thuốc* (pharmacy) is the first place people go for minor complaints. The pharmacist usually listens to your symptoms and hands you medicine on the spot, and many drugs that need a prescription elsewhere can be bought here. For minor problems it's very convenient; for anything that doesn't improve in two or three days, do go to a *bệnh viện* (hospital) or *phòng khám* (clinic).
The parting words you'll hear: *Chúc em mau khỏi nhé!* — "get well soon". Just answer *Em cảm ơn chị ạ.* And when a friend of yours is sick, this is the sentence they're waiting to hear from you.
